questions.question: A prototype in product development serves to:

options.A: Be the final product delivered to customers
options.B: Test and validate design concepts before full development investment
options.C: Replace all forms of user testing

questions.explanation: Test and validate design concepts before full development investment. Explanation: Prototypes are early models — paper, wireframe, or digital — used to test ideas cheaply and gather feedback before committing to full development.

questions.question: A Minimum Viable Product (MVP) is:

options.A: The most feature-rich version of a product
options.B: The final polished version ready for mass market
options.C: The simplest version with just enough features to satisfy early users and validate core assumptions
options.D: A product that requires no testing

questions.explanation: The simplest version with just enough features to satisfy early users and validate core assumptions. Explanation: MVP enables rapid market entry — feedback from early users guides future development without over-investing upfront.

questions.question: Iterative design in prototyping means:

options.A: Designing the product only once with no changes
options.B: Repeatedly refining the design based on testing and user feedback in cycles
options.C: Making the product as complex as possible initially
options.D: Outsourcing all design to external agencies

questions.explanation: Repeatedly refining the design based on testing and user feedback in cycles. Explanation: Iterative design cycles through: design, prototype, test, evaluate, and refine — improving the product with each loop.

questions.question: User testing is valuable in product development because:

options.A: It eliminates the need for prototypes
options.B: It guarantees commercial success
options.C: It reveals real usability problems that developers overlooked before the product is fully built

questions.explanation: It reveals real usability problems that developers overlooked before the product is fully built. Explanation: User testing uncovers issues with navigation, clarity, and functionality — preventing costly post-launch fixes.

questions.question: Prioritisation when developing an MVP means:

options.A: Including every possible feature
options.B: Selecting only the essential features that deliver the core value proposition
options.C: Developing the most technically complex features first

questions.explanation: Selecting only the essential features that deliver the core value proposition. Explanation: MVP prioritisation focuses on the smallest feature set that solves the core problem — everything else is deferred based on feedback.

questions.question: The Build-Measure-Learn cycle is associated with:

options.A: The Waterfall Model
options.B: Lean Startup methodology
options.C: Six Sigma

questions.explanation: Lean Startup methodology. Explanation: The Lean Startup's Build-Measure-Learn loop: build an MVP, measure real user responses, learn whether to persevere or pivot.

questions.question: A wireframe in product design is:

options.A: A high-fidelity visual mockup with colours and images
options.B: A basic skeletal layout showing structure and UI elements without visual styling
options.C: The final manufactured product

questions.explanation: A basic skeletal layout showing structure and UI elements without visual styling. Explanation: Wireframes are low-fidelity blueprints — they define layout and navigation structure without design details like colour or typography.

questions.question: What does 'pivot' mean in entrepreneurship?

options.A: Improving the current product's marketing only
options.B: Changing the product's fundamental direction based on validated learning from user feedback
options.C: Launching a second product simultaneously

questions.explanation: Changing the product's fundamental direction based on validated learning from user feedback. Explanation: A pivot is a strategic course correction — the team and core technology remain, but the product direction changes based on evidence.

questions.question: Intellectual property (IP) in product development refers to:

options.A: Physical hardware components
options.B: Competitor products
options.C: Legal rights protecting creative inventions, designs, software, and brand identity

questions.explanation: Legal rights protecting creative inventions, designs, software, and brand identity. Explanation: IP includes patents (inventions), copyrights (creative works), trademarks (brand identity), and trade secrets.

questions.question: Market research in entrepreneurship is conducted primarily to:

options.A: Design the company logo
options.B: Write the application code
options.C: Understand customer needs, market size, and competition before building a product

questions.explanation: Understand customer needs, market size, and competition before building a product. Explanation: Market research validates whether a business idea solves a real problem and whether sufficient demand exists before investing resources.

questions.question: Design thinking is a problem-solving approach that is primarily:

options.A: Technology-centred
options.B: Data-centred
options.C: Human-centred — starting with deep empathy for the user's real needs

questions.explanation: Human-centred — starting with deep empathy for the user's real needs. Explanation: Design thinking begins with Empathise — understanding users deeply — before defining problems and generating solutions.

questions.question: The correct order of Design Thinking's five stages is:

options.A: Prototype, Test, Ideate, Define, Empathise
options.B: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test
options.C: Define, Empathise, Prototype, Ideate, Test

questions.explanation: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test. Explanation: Design Thinking: (1) Empathise with users, (2) Define the problem, (3) Ideate solutions, (4) Prototype, (5) Test.

questions.question: A SWOT analysis in a business plan identifies:

options.A: Software, Web, Operations, Technology
options.B: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
options.C: Systems, Workflows, Objectives, Tasks

questions.explanation: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats. Explanation: SWOT analysis evaluates internal factors (Strengths, Weaknesses) and external factors (Opportunities, Threats) facing a business.

questions.question: A Unique Selling Proposition (USP) defines:

options.A: The technical architecture of the product
options.B: What makes the product distinctly better or different from all competitors
options.C: The total addressable market size
options.D: The number of features in the MVP

questions.explanation: What makes the product distinctly better or different from all competitors. Explanation: A clear USP answers 'why should customers choose this over alternatives?' — essential for positioning and marketing.

questions.question: In the MoSCoW prioritisation framework, 'M' stands for:

options.A: Manageable
options.B: Minimum
options.C: Must Have

questions.explanation: Must Have. Explanation: MoSCoW: Must Have (essential features), Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have (this time) — used to prioritise MVP scope.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes a product in business? ★

options.A: An intangible idea that has not yet been developed
options.B: A physical or tangible item created to meet a specific need or want of consumers
options.C: A marketing plan for a business

questions.explanation: A physical or tangible item created to meet a specific need or want of consumers. Explanation: Products are typically physical items — smartphones, clothing, automobiles, and consumer electronics — that can be seen, touched, or held. They differ from services, which are intangible offerings.

questions.question: Why is successful product development considered a cornerstone of business sustainability? ★

options.A: It allows companies to avoid paying taxes
options.B: It brings new products to market effectively and efficiently, generating revenue and maintaining competitive advantage
options.C: It eliminates the need for any marketing effort
options.D: It guarantees that competitors will copy the product

questions.explanation: It brings new products to market effectively and efficiently, generating revenue and maintaining competitive advantage. Explanation: Successful product development drives revenue generation, customer satisfaction, innovation, and market expansion — all of which are essential for a business to remain competitive and sustainable long-term.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of product development listed in the textbook? ★

options.A: It eliminates the need for customer feedback
options.B: It allows companies to enter new markets and expand their customer base
options.C: It reduces the company's need to innovate
options.D: It guarantees that the product will be profitable immediately

questions.explanation: It allows companies to enter new markets and expand their customer base. Explanation: Market expansion is one of the key benefits of product development. Developing new products or services allows a company to explore new markets and demographics, further diversifying its business and reducing dependence on a single product.

questions.question: Entrepreneurship requires which of the following key qualities? ★

options.A: Avoiding all forms of risk and uncertainty
options.B: Skills, qualities, and traits to undertake risks and successfully launch a business
options.C: Following existing business models without any innovation
options.D: Waiting until all risks are eliminated before starting

questions.explanation: Skills, qualities, and traits to undertake risks and successfully launch a business. Explanation: Entrepreneurship involves calculated risk-taking combined with skills and drive. Successful entrepreneurs are willing to face uncertainty, learn from failure, and persist in building their vision into a viable business.

questions.question: How does successful product development contribute to customer satisfaction? ★

options.A: By offering the lowest possible price regardless of quality
options.B: By addressing specific customer needs and wants, making the product the preferred choice
options.C: By copying competitors' products exactly
options.D: By reducing the number of features to simplify the product

questions.explanation: By addressing specific customer needs and wants, making the product the preferred choice. Explanation: Products that genuinely solve customer problems and meet their needs create satisfaction and loyalty. A well-developed product that addresses real pain points is more likely to be adopted and recommended by users.

questions.question: Which type of prototype is described as a simple, hand-drawn or digital representation focusing on basic layout and flow? ★

options.A: High-fidelity digital prototype
options.B: Alpha prototype
options.C: Low-fidelity sketch or wireframe

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity sketch or wireframe. Explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes — sketches and wireframes — are quick and inexpensive to create. They focus on basic layout, structure, and flow without detailed design, making them ideal for early-stage ideation and concept validation.

questions.question: A paper prototype is classified as which level of fidelity? ★

options.A: High-fidelity
options.B: Low-fidelity
options.C: Functional prototype

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity. Explanation: Paper prototypes use physical materials like paper and cardboard to create interactive models. They offer more detail than rough sketches but are still low-fidelity — inexpensive, quick to build, and suitable for early user feedback.

questions.question: A digital prototype that closely resembles the final product's user interface and functionality is classified as: ★

options.A: A low-fidelity wireframe
options.B: A paper prototype
options.C: A high-fidelity digital prototype

questions.explanation: A high-fidelity digital prototype. Explanation: High-fidelity digital prototypes are interactive, computer-generated simulations that closely resemble the final product. They are used for detailed user testing, usability studies, and investor or stakeholder presentations.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a proof-of-concept prototype? ★

options.A: To present a complete, finished product to customers
options.B: To demonstrate the core functionality and technical feasibility of a product concept
options.C: To replace beta testing
options.D: To finalise the product's visual design and branding

questions.explanation: To demonstrate the core functionality and technical feasibility of a product concept. Explanation: Proof-of-concept prototypes test whether the core technology or idea actually works — they may lack aesthetic polish but confirm that the fundamental concept is technically achievable before further investment.

questions.question: An alpha prototype is best described as: ★

options.A: A rough sketch of the product idea
options.B: A near-final version released to a select group of external users
options.C: An advanced, functional version with most features in place, used for internal testing and refinement
options.D: A digital wireframe with no interactive elements

questions.explanation: An advanced, functional version with most features in place, used for internal testing and refinement. Explanation: Alpha prototypes are advanced working versions used internally by the development team to test and refine the product before it is shown to any external users or released for wider testing.

questions.question: Beta prototypes differ from alpha prototypes in that beta prototypes: ★

options.A: Are only hand-drawn sketches
options.B: Are released internally to the development team only
options.C: Are near-final versions made available to a select group of external users to identify remaining issues before official release
options.D: Are the simplest possible version of the product

questions.explanation: Are near-final versions made available to a select group of external users to identify remaining issues before official release. Explanation: Beta testing involves real external users who test the near-complete product. Their feedback identifies remaining bugs, usability issues, and edge cases that the internal team may have missed during alpha testing.

questions.question: How does prototyping support investor and stakeholder confidence? ★

options.A: By replacing the need for financial projections
options.B: By providing a realistic preview of the final product's capabilities through high-fidelity prototypes
options.C: By guaranteeing that the product will generate profit
options.D: By eliminating all technical risks from the project

questions.explanation: By providing a realistic preview of the final product's capabilities through high-fidelity prototypes. Explanation: High-fidelity prototypes allow investors and stakeholders to see and interact with a realistic representation of the final product. This tangible demonstration builds confidence in the concept and increases the likelihood of securing funding.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why prototyping is important in product development? ★

options.A: It helps identify design flaws before full production
options.B: It supports user-centred design by gathering early feedback
options.C: It guarantees that the final product will be commercially successful
options.D: It reduces the cost of errors by catching problems early

questions.explanation: It guarantees that the final product will be commercially successful. Explanation: Prototyping reduces risk and improves quality, but it cannot guarantee commercial success — that depends on market conditions, pricing, competition, and many other factors beyond design quality.

questions.question: Which software tools are used for creating interactive digital prototypes with realistic user interfaces? ★

options.A: Microsoft Word and Excel
options.B: Adobe XD, Sketch, Figma, or InVision
options.C: Python and Java

questions.explanation: Adobe XD, Sketch, Figma, or InVision. Explanation: Design and prototyping tools like Adobe XD, Sketch, Figma, and InVision allow designers to create interactive digital prototypes with realistic layouts, navigation flows, and user interface elements — without writing actual code.

questions.question: Which tools are used for creating 3D digital models of physical products? ★

options.A: Adobe XD and Figma
options.B: HTML and CSS
options.C: Autodesk Fusion 360 or Blender

questions.explanation: Autodesk Fusion 360 or Blender. Explanation: 3D modelling software like Autodesk Fusion 360 and Blender enable designers and engineers to create detailed three-dimensional digital models of physical products before manufacturing them.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 3D printer in prototype development? ★

options.A: To scan existing objects and convert them to digital files
options.B: To transform digital 3D designs into physical, tangible prototype objects
options.C: To run software simulations of product behaviour

questions.explanation: To transform digital 3D designs into physical, tangible prototype objects. Explanation: 3D printers take a digital 3D model and produce a physical object layer by layer. This allows designers and engineers to hold, test, and evaluate a real physical version of their product design quickly and cost-effectively.

questions.question: Which material is commonly used for building LOW-COST, low-fidelity physical prototypes? ★

options.A: Titanium and carbon fibre
options.B: Cardboard and foam board
options.C: Precious metals

questions.explanation: Cardboard and foam board. Explanation: Cardboard and foam board are inexpensive, easy to cut, and shape — making them ideal for quickly building rough physical models that communicate size, form, and layout without significant cost or time investment.

questions.question: What is an Arduino kit used for in prototype development? ★

options.A: Creating digital wireframes and mockups
options.B: Building electronics prototypes with programmable microcontrollers
options.C: Designing 3D models of physical products

questions.explanation: Building electronics prototypes with programmable microcontrollers. Explanation: Arduino kits are specialised prototyping kits that include programmable microcontrollers, sensors, and electronic components. They are used to prototype IoT devices, robotics, and other electronic products quickly.

questions.question: In the iterative design process, what happens AFTER gathering feedback from users? ★

options.A: The project is cancelled if any negative feedback is received
options.B: The feedback is ignored and the original design is kept
options.C: The data is analysed, necessary changes are made to the prototype, and testing is repeated
options.D: The product is immediately launched to the market

questions.explanation: The data is analysed, necessary changes are made to the prototype, and testing is repeated. Explanation: Iterative design follows a cycle: gather feedback, analyse data, identify improvements, make changes to the prototype, and then test again. This cycle repeats until the design meets the desired goals and user needs.

questions.question: Documentation during iterative prototyping is important because: ★

options.A: It replaces the need for any user testing
options.B: It records changes, decisions, and rationale made during each iteration for reference and future development
options.C: It is required by law for all product development projects
options.D: It automatically generates the final product code

questions.explanation: It records changes, decisions, and rationale made during each iteration for reference and future development. Explanation: Documenting each design iteration creates a record of what was changed, why, and what the outcome was. This historical record is valuable for team alignment, future development phases, and understanding the design evolution.

questions.question: What types of data are collected during prototype user testing? ★

options.A: Only financial projections and budget data
options.B: Both quantitative data (e.g., task completion rates, time spent) and qualitative data (e.g., user comments, observations)
options.C: Only written survey responses in multiple choice format
options.D: Only technical performance metrics from the server

questions.explanation: Both quantitative data (e.g., task completion rates, time spent) and qualitative data (e.g., user comments, observations). Explanation: Comprehensive user testing collects both types of data. Quantitative data provides measurable metrics, while qualitative data captures the nuanced experiences and opinions that numbers alone cannot convey.

questions.question: After identifying issues through user testing, what is the CORRECT next step? ★

options.A: Immediately launch the product regardless of the issues
options.B: Prioritise issues by severity and impact, then make iterative changes to the prototype
options.C: Discard the prototype and start from scratch
options.D: Only fix issues that users complained about loudly

questions.explanation: Prioritise issues by severity and impact, then make iterative changes to the prototype. Explanation: Not all issues have equal importance. Critical usability problems must be addressed first. Changes are then made to the prototype and it is re-tested — continuing the iterative cycle until the product meets quality goals.

questions.question: Validation in user testing refers to: ★

options.A: Confirming that the product's branding is attractive
options.B: Checking whether the product's design assumptions and concept effectively solve the intended problem
options.C: Ensuring all team members have approved the design
options.D: Verifying that the product code compiles without errors

questions.explanation: Checking whether the product's design assumptions and concept effectively solve the intended problem. Explanation: Validation confirms that the product concept actually works as intended for real users. It tests whether design decisions were correct and whether the product genuinely solves the problem it was designed to address.

questions.question: Usability testing specifically focuses on: ★

options.A: Testing the product's server performance and uptime
options.B: Evaluating the financial viability of the business model
options.C: How users interact with the product — assessing interface clarity, navigation, and overall user experience
options.D: Checking whether the product complies with legal regulations

questions.explanation: How users interact with the product — assessing interface clarity, navigation, and overall user experience. Explanation: Usability testing observes real users attempting to complete tasks with the product. It identifies where users struggle, get confused, or make errors — providing actionable insights to improve the interface and experience.

questions.question: Why is re-testing the prototype after making changes an important step? ★

options.A: To confirm that no new issues were introduced and that previous issues have been resolved
options.B: To meet legal requirements for product launches
options.C: To demonstrate the product to investors
options.D: To generate marketing content for the product launch

questions.explanation: To confirm that no new issues were introduced and that previous issues have been resolved. Explanation: Re-testing after changes validates that the fixes worked correctly and checks that the modifications did not accidentally introduce new problems. This verification step is essential in the iterative improvement cycle.

questions.question: Feature creep in MVP development refers to: ★

options.A: Adding too few features to the minimum viable product
options.B: The gradual, uncontrolled addition of features beyond the core scope, making the product unnecessarily complex
options.C: A bug caused by conflicting product features
options.D: The process of prioritising essential features first

questions.explanation: The gradual, uncontrolled addition of features beyond the core scope, making the product unnecessarily complex. Explanation: Feature creep undermines the purpose of an MVP. The goal is to stay lean and focused on the core value. Each added feature increases development time, cost, and complexity — and may distract from solving the core problem.

questions.question: What does scalability mean in the context of MVP development? ★

options.A: Designing the MVP to be as small as possible with no future growth potential
options.B: Building the MVP's architecture in a way that allows it to handle growth and future enhancements
options.C: Making the MVP available in multiple languages at launch
options.D: Reducing the number of users who can access the MVP

questions.explanation: Building the MVP's architecture in a way that allows it to handle growth and future enhancements. Explanation: Even though an MVP is minimal, its technical foundation should be designed with scalability in mind. As the user base grows and new features are added, the system must be able to expand without requiring a complete rebuild.

questions.question: Agile development methodology is used in MVP development because: ★

options.A: It requires all features to be planned and locked in before development begins
options.B: It allows for flexibility in responding to changing requirements and user feedback through rapid, iterative development
options.C: It eliminates the need for any user testing
options.D: It guarantees that the product will be completed on time and within budget

questions.explanation: It allows for flexibility in responding to changing requirements and user feedback through rapid, iterative development. Explanation: Agile methodology breaks development into short sprints, allowing teams to continuously incorporate feedback and adapt to change. This flexibility is essential for MVP development, where learning from early users drives the product's direction.

questions.question: User onboarding in an MVP refers to: ★

options.A: The process of hiring new team members
options.B: Making it easy for new users to understand and effectively use the product from their first interaction
options.C: The legal process of registering the product
options.D: Collecting user payment information at registration

questions.explanation: Making it easy for new users to understand and effectively use the product from their first interaction. Explanation: Good user onboarding guides new users through the product's key features and value. Poor onboarding leads to user confusion and early abandonment — even if the product itself is valuable.

questions.question: Which of the following is the MAIN purpose of launching an MVP? ★

options.A: To impress investors with a polished, complete product
options.B: To validate core assumptions with real users and gather feedback to guide further development
options.C: To eliminate all competition in the market
options.D: To finalise the product's branding and visual identity

questions.explanation: To validate core assumptions with real users and gather feedback to guide further development. Explanation: An MVP is launched to learn — not to be perfect. Real user interactions reveal whether the core assumptions were correct. This feedback determines whether to persevere with the current direction, pivot, or discontinue. questions.question: A startup team sketches their app idea on paper and tests it with five colleagues. This is an example of: ★

options.A: A beta prototype
options.B: A high-fidelity digital prototype
options.C: A low-fidelity paper prototype

questions.explanation: A low-fidelity paper prototype. Explanation: Paper sketches tested with a small group represent the earliest, lowest-fidelity form of prototyping. This approach is fast and cheap — perfect for validating basic layout and flow ideas before investing in digital development.

questions.question: A team discovers during user testing that users cannot find the navigation menu. The CORRECT response is to: ★

options.A: Launch the product anyway and fix it in the next version
options.B: Ignore the feedback as users will eventually learn
options.C: Treat this as a critical usability issue, redesign the navigation, and re-test

questions.explanation: Treat this as a critical usability issue, redesign the navigation, and re- test Explanation: Navigation is fundamental to usability. An inability to find the menu is a critical issue that would prevent users from using the product effectively. It must be prioritised, fixed, and re- tested before launch.

questions.question: A company builds an app with only its three most essential features and releases it to 100 early users. This is an example of: ★

options.A: A high-fidelity prototype
options.B: A SWOT analysis
options.C: A minimum viable product (MVP)

questions.explanation: A minimum viable product (MVP). Explanation: Releasing a stripped-down version with only essential features to early users is the definition of an MVP. The goal is to validate the core concept with real users and gather feedback before investing in full development.

questions.question: During SWOT analysis, a company identifies that it has no established brand recognition. This is classified as: ★

options.A: An opportunity
options.B: A strength
options.C: A threat

questions.explanation: A weakness. Explanation: Weaknesses are internal factors that put the company at a disadvantage — things it lacks or does poorly. No brand recognition is an internal weakness because it makes it harder to attract customers compared to established competitors.

questions.question: A food delivery startup realises that their original idea — restaurant bookings — has poor demand, but their logistics platform is valuable for package delivery. Changing direction is called: ★

options.A: Prototyping
options.B: Pivoting
options.C: Scaling

questions.explanation: Pivoting. Explanation: A pivot is a strategic change in direction based on validated learning. The team keeps their core technology (logistics platform) but applies it to a different market (package delivery) where real demand exists.

questions.question: A designer uses Figma to create a fully interactive mockup of a mobile app with realistic colours, icons, and animations. This is classified as: ★

options.A: A low-fidelity wireframe
options.B: A paper prototype
options.C: A high-fidelity digital prototype

questions.explanation: A high-fidelity digital prototype. Explanation: A fully interactive mockup with realistic visual design created in a professional design tool is a high-fidelity digital prototype. It closely resembles the final product and is suitable for investor presentations and detailed user testing.

questions.question: Which stage of Design Thinking involves generating a wide range of creative solutions to the defined problem without immediately judging or filtering ideas? ★

options.A: Empathise
options.B: Define
options.C: Ideate

questions.explanation: Ideate. Explanation: The Ideate stage encourages divergent thinking — generating as many potential solutions as possible without evaluation. Quantity is prioritised over quality at this stage, with filtering and selection coming later.
